p.t: In short
p.s: Selling the business: legal, tax and transaction matters

p.t: Keep clean, complete financial records from day one. Buyers often want **four years** of them.
Choose before listing: **asset sale** (you sell parts of the business) or stock sale (you sell the whole company). Asset sales are simpler.
Use **escrow** (a neutral holder keeps the money until the transfer is checked) to protect both sides.
A broker's fee is **15%** on stores under $1 million. A private sale avoids that fee, but you lose the broker's buyer list and protections.
Preparing the store for sale
p.s: Selling the business: legal, tax and transaction matters

p.t: Keep accurate, complete books (the record of all money in and out) from the start.
Brokers and marketplaces usually require **several years** of complete financial records. The example given was four years. Older guidance from 2021 to 2022 gives the same requirement.
Store **all supplier invoices** (bills from your product suppliers) in Google Drive, so they are easy to show during buyer due diligence (the buyer's own checks before buying) and verification.
Turn off **WHOIS privacy (the setting that hides your name in the public record of who owns a web address) in the last month** before listing. Your own name must show as domain owner.
Buyers look up WHOIS to confirm ownership.
**Make sure you can be verified** as a seller: real social profiles with real friends, and a LinkedIn profile (a professional networking site) with genuine connections.
Sellers without an online presence may be asked for ID, a passport or a social security card, which makes the sale harder.
**Decide before listing** (putting the store up for sale) whether you will do an asset sale (specific assets transfer)

or a stock sale (transfer of ownership of the entire company).
Asset sales are simpler. Stock sales require deeper buyer due diligence.
On this marketplace, **more than nine out of ten** sales are asset sales.
Websites, files and domains are transferred, but the LLC (a company type that separates the owner's personal money from the business) stays with the seller.
A stock sale of an LLC requires much deeper due diligence, because the buyer must consider lawsuits arising from earlier actions.
The usual way to sell a store is an **asset sale** in which the LLC sells the Shopify store (the online shop platform), ad account access, supplier contacts and email lists.
The LLC stays with the owner and can be dissolved (closed down) or reused later. This is older advice from 2022.
You typically **do not have to sell your LLC** structure.
Buyers conduct more extensive due diligence when purchasing an LLC than when purchasing specific assets.
Large portfolio buyers (people who own many stores) usually set up a **separate LLC for each store**, which makes record keeping straightforward. This setup is common among portfolio buyers.
Trademark risk in listings
p.s: Selling the business: legal, tax and transaction matters

p.t: A business with a **partially trademarked name** (a brand name that is partly legally protected) can be listed for sale.
Some buyers may avoid it because of perceived legal risk.
A partially trademarked name can be listed if the seller has not received a **warning or cease and desist** (a formal legal letter demanding you stop).

**Avoid well-known brands**, such as Marvel, in listings.
Some buyers may still be uncomfortable with the risk, even when the listing is allowed.
A **broker is a middleman who finds buyers for you for a fee. A private sale means you find and handle the buyer yourself.**

**Earn-out** means part of the price is paid later, from future profit.
**Sale price**

Brokerage: Typically higher, through professional buyer matching.
Private sale: You keep the full sales price.
**Negotiation**

Brokerage: Broker guides you through negotiations and earn-out scenarios.
Private sale: You handle negotiation yourself.
**Buyer qualification**

Brokerage: Broker qualifies buyers to protect your time.
Private sale: Harder to qualify serious buyers.
**Competitors**
Brokerage: Broker screens competitors using deposit systems (required up-front payments from buyers).

Private sale: Financial records are exposed to potential competitors.
**Migration**
Brokerage: Broker handles business migration (moving the store, accounts and domain to the buyer).

Private sale: You are responsible for business migration.
**Buyer list and protections**
Brokerage: Broker's buyer list and protections apply.

Private sale: No broker buyer list or protections.
**Fee**
Brokerage: **15%** of the sales price.
Private sale: No broker fee.
Broker Fees
p.s: Selling the business: legal, tax and transaction matters

p.t: Brokerage commission (the broker's fee) on dropshipping store sales under $1 million is **15%** of the final sale price.
The broker charges a fee of **15%** of the sales price, which the source describes as standard in the industry.
Private sales avoid this fee, but they lack the broker's buyer list and protections.
**Escrow protects both sides by holding the buyer's money until the site has been fully transferred and checked**.
The seller is paid only after the new owner confirms that everything works.
Third-party escrow services (outside companies that hold the money) such as escrow.com move money safely but do not handle the migration.
Moving the store, its accounts and its domain still needs someone to manage the details.
An escrow service can protect a private sale when everything goes smoothly.
Escrow services are not specialised in online businesses, so **arbitration** (settling a dispute through an independent decision-maker instead of a court) can be difficult if a problem arises.
A broker that holds the buyer's funds until the transfer is complete may not be allowed to call itself an escrow company under US banking rules.
**Before paying, confirm how the money is held** and whether the arrangement is legally valid in your jurisdiction (the country or region whose laws apply).
Buyers must complete due diligence themselves.
The sale platform **vets** (checks) listings before publication, but the responsibility to check suppliers, relationships and whether the business suits them stays with the buyer.
**Prepare records** that answer a buyer's checks on suppliers, relationships and the store's history. The buyer will run these checks regardless of the platform's vetting.
**Addbacks** (costs you add back to profit) allow you to reintroduce expenses from your tax return into net profit (profit after costs) for valuation

(working out the price) when they differ from what a buyer would actually incur.
Prepare to justify and negotiate these adjustments.
Seller financing and earn-Outs
p.s: Selling the business: legal, tax and transaction matters

p.t: **Seller financing** (the seller accepts payment over time instead of all at once), such as an earn-out or a share of profits paid over several months,
becomes more common as deal sizes grow. It bridges the gap between the buyer's ability to pay upfront and the seller's asking price.
Seller financing can take the form of an earn-out or a share of profits over several months, for example **$5,000** per month for six months.
In this structure, the broker holds the domain until the buyer makes the **final payment**. The broker can transfer it back or use it as leverage (a bargaining tool) if the buyer breaks the contract.
When buying or selling a business, the buyer should require a **non-compete agreement** (a signed promise that the seller will not run a
similar business). Without one, the seller can open the same niche (product market) again soon after the sale. This is older advice from 2020.
Observed non-compete terms ranged from **12 months to 5 years**. This is older advice from 2020.
Transferring accounts to a buyer in another country can take **months**.
One American buyer who had to set up an EU company (a company registered in the European Union) for an EU migration was three months into a migration that was not going smoothly.
**Check cross-border handovers early.**
1. The seller **submits** the store for vetting (checking), and a team reviews it.
p.h: Deal process on a broker platform

p.t:
2. Once approved, the store is **listed** (put up for sale).
3. The sales team **screens** buyer interest.
4. A **prep call** with the seller takes place.

5. A **buyer-seller call** led by the broker takes place.
6. A **post-call follow-up** with the seller takes place.
7. The broker helps **negotiate**.
8. After the **asset purchase agreement** (the signed contract for buying the assets) is signed, the broker's team migrates the business and hands it over.
